content:
SatWiki Research is a public notebook on how satellites actually work. Two kinds of writing live here: news posts that record events such as launches, constellation deployments, policy decisions and failures, and longer explainers that cover the physics and engineering behind them.
Everything is filed by theme:
News - reverse chronological; each post states what happened, when, and on what evidence. Space Systems - long-form pieces with tables, formulas and diagrams, grouped into series that can be read in order. Tools - small utilities that run in the browser, such as the TLE two-line element parser. The fuller reference wiki sits at sat.huijiwiki.com. The two are complementary: that site carries encyclopedic entries, this one carries launch news and technical write-ups.

content:
A two-line element set (TLE) is a fixed-width text format inherited from NORAD. Its constraint is not what the text means but where each character sits: every line is exactly 69 characters wide, field widths are fixed, decimal points are usually omitted, and one column is given over to a checksum. Parsers that fail usually drift by one column rather than miscompute a number.
Fields on line 1#Column Width Meaning 1 1 Line number, always 1 3 to 7 5 Satellite number (NORAD catalogue number) 8 1 Classification: U unclassified, C classified, S secret 10 to 11 2 Last two digits of the international designator launch year 12 to 14 3 Launch number of that year 15 to 17 3 Piece of that launch 19 to 20 2 Last two digits of the epoch year 21 to 32 12 Epoch: day of the year plus its fractional part 34 to 43 10 First derivative of mean motion 45 to 52 8 Second derivative of mean motion 54 to 61 8 BSTAR drag term 63 1 Ephemeris type, normally 0 65 to 68 4 Element set number, incremented on every update 69 1 Checksum Columns 2, 9, 18, 33, 44, 53, 62 and 64 hold spaces and nothing else. A parser that reads past them without accounting for them is off by one from that point onwards.
Fields on line 2#Column Width Meaning 1 1 Line number, always 2 3 to 7 5 Satellite number, must match line 1 9 to 16 8 Inclination, degrees 18 to 25 8 Right ascension of the ascending node, degrees 27 to 33 7 Eccentricity, with the leading 0. dropped: 1234567 means 0.1234567 35 to 42 8 Argument of perigee, degrees 44 to 51 8 Mean anomaly, degrees 53 to 63 11 Mean motion, revolutions per day 64 to 68 5 Revolution number at epoch 69 1 Checksum Two traps sit here. Eccentricity has to be read as a fraction, with 0. put back before the digits. Mean motion is in revolutions per day, so converting to angular rate means multiplying by 360 degrees, and converting to a period means taking the reciprocal and rescaling to seconds.
The derivative and BSTAR fields use the same shorthand in a different form: 12345-4 stands for 0.12345 times ten to the minus four, with the mantissa’s decimal point and the exponent letter both left out.
The checksum#The checksum covers the first 68 characters. Digits count as their face value, a minus sign counts as one, a decimal point counts as one, everything else counts as zero. The total is taken modulo 10 and written into the last column.
A mismatch usually means the line was truncated or shifted in transmission, not that the orbit data itself is wrong.
How the numbers get used#A TLE holds mean elements, so it cannot be used directly as an instantaneous set for high-precision extrapolation. For position prediction, a model such as SGP4 converts the mean elements into an osculating state, and the propagation time since epoch is added on top. The further the request sits from epoch, the faster the error grows, which shows up most sharply for low Earth orbit objects.
The TLE analyzer on this site cuts a line by column and prints each field, which makes it a convenient reference when checking a custom parser.
summary: A column-by-column reading of the fixed-width TLE format: what each field means, where the decimal point is implied, and how the checksum is computed.
title: The 69-column layout of a TLE line

content:
Before this change sat-wiki.github.io held a few loose pages: an interactive script under /chunqiu/, a TLE analyzer under /tools/, and no home page at all, so the bare domain returned 404. The whole site now builds with Hugo on the Blowfish theme, which gives news and technical posts a shared list view, taxonomy and RSS feed.
What changed:
Source and output are separate. The Hugo project lives in src/; the built files are published to the repository root, which is where GitHub Pages has always read from, so no repository setting had to move. Old URLs survive. /chunqiu/, /tools/tle_data_analyzer.html and the font files moved into src/static/, and the build writes them back to the same paths. Existing external links keep working. Two kinds of content. /news/ holds dated posts in reverse order; /space-systems/ holds long-form technical pieces with tables of contents, formulas, code and series grouping. Both appear in the feed. The toolchain is pinned. Blowfish v3 requires Hugo Extended 0.162 or newer; this build used 0.169. The theme is a git submodule, so upgrading means moving the submodule pointer. Day-to-day maintenance: edit the Markdown under src/content/, then run ./deploy.ps1 to build and push.
summary: sat-wiki.github.io went from a handful of hand-written pages to a Hugo build, with source and output kept apart and old URLs left in place.
title: The site moves to Hugo and Blowfish

content:
SatWiki Research is a public notebook on space technology. It is written for people who need to check a single launch date or who want to understand how a particular orbit or subsystem behaves.
The material is split three ways:
News (/news/) records events and dates, with the evidence stated. Commentary stays out. Space Systems (/space-systems/) explains how things work, in long form with tables, formulas and diagrams, filed into series. Tools (/tools/) holds utilities that run in the browser, such as the TLE parser. The encyclopedic coverage lives on the community wiki at sat.huijiwiki.com. This site complements it: entries there, launch news and technical write-ups here.
The source is on GitHub, built with Hugo and Blowfish. Issues pointing out errors are welcome.
